text:
Minecraft had a similar problem even before AI drove the slop into overdrive. MCreator marketed itself as a code free means to create mods, and soon cookie cutter clickbait flooded the listings. The problems came swiftly as MCreator wasn't optimised and created numerous bugs or incompatibilities that the 'modder' couldn't fix without knowing how to code. They effectively became a liability to pack devs who would be refused support if one of these slop mods were involved. 

Now we have AI accelerating the same slop for all games, with even shittier code, in a race to the bottom for the most clickbait garbage imaginable. These so called 'mash-ups' aren't built to play nice with other handcrafted mods, and almost certainly won't be maintained beyond their short-lived hypecycle.

It's all pump & dump mods cashing out before the waning novelty can't outweigh the shitty quality.

TL;DR: This is impressive, however for me personally seeing cool Bethesda mods is so bittersweet at this point. Like imagine the kinds of things you could do if you put that effort into somewhere more appreciated. Idk.

I certainly don't mean to insult anyone's efforts, I imagine Bethesda games do offer some real value for budding game developers in the form of a very accessible entrypoint into modding and I think that's great. 

But what would be even better is if this company weren't basically entirely surviving off the coat tails of their community of unpaid laborers. The only reason why these games are so moddable is because Bethesda as a company wouldn't survive if they weren't. The product being given by itself is so bad and Bethesda so inept that it _compelled_ people to learn how to fix it themselves just to deliver on what could've been. 

Bethesda basically sells you the idea of a game, delivers about 60% of it and then asks you to make up the difference. Anyone playing Skyrim or Fallout 4 could see how good those games could've been even with no prior game design knowledge, it's just an innate feeling.

text:
A console business largely lives and dies by how many customers it has in the first place, so cutting out double digit percentages of them sounds like a hell of a bad idea to me.  As an anecdote, I've got friends who buy plenty of digital games on consoles because there is no physical option, but when physical is an option, they do so.  That sounds like you could easily convince them to just buy everything on digital then, right?  Well, maybe not.  If physical is never an option, they'd wonder why they bother with a console in the first place, since they can't save money on used copies (either selling a new copy and recouping some cost or buying used at a discount) ever.  At that point, why not just play on PC where the online is free and the discounts are better?  With no disc drive, they lose most of their reason for playing on console at all.

Anyway, it looks stupid to me to cut out the physical market in the 2020s, and I haven't even bought a physical game for 4 years.
